Alien Registration
Within 90 days of your arrival in Korea, you must register to get an Alien Registration Card regardless of your visa type unless your total period of stay in Korea is less than 90 days. The International Center provides exchange students with this service.
Upon your arrival, please submit the following documents:
Completed Application Form (application form is available at the International Center)
One color photos [3x4]
(The Background must be a white color.)
Passport
Certificate of Enrollment
A copy of Housing Contract
Tuberculosis(TB) Test Result
(※ TB Test result is required only for those who applied to stay at Inha dormitory during their academic semester(s).)
Photocopy of Insurance Policy
Application Fee: KRW 30,000
Student ID
The student ID card is both your student identification card and your library card. It is issued to all Inha students in order to access resources such as campus libraries and photocopying.
The student ID card would be issued prior to the beginning of a semester. Distribution date and pick-up location will be announced via Inha University website (Inha New>notice) or e-mail.

Visiting Students & Student Exchange Program
SMWU’s Semester Abroad Program offers a unique opportunity for university students currently enrolled in institutions outside of Korea. Both male and female students are eligible to apply. As a Study Abroad student, you can earn credits towards your home degree while immersing yourself in a valuable international and intercultural experience in Korea. Additionally, Exchange Students from Partner Institutions have the option to participate in this program, with the possibility of tuition waiver based on the exchange agreement. Participants in the program have the chance to enroll in SMWU’s undergraduate and graduate schools. Earned credits are recorded on an official SMWU transcript, which may be transferable to other universities.

Academic Calendar
Sookmyung Women’s University operates on a two-semester academic year. The spring semester runs from March to mid-June, while the fall semester takes place from September to mid-December. In addition to these regular semesters, Summer Sessions are offered prior to the fall semester.

Courses
We offer over 150 English-taught courses in various disciplines at both undergraduate and graduate levels. Students can choose from a range of subjects such as Korean language, International Studies, Korean Studies, Business and Economics and more. Additionally, there are numerous opportunities to engage in traditional Korean culture through lectures and field trips. For a complete course list and descriptions, please visit: [Click here-

How to apply
Entry Requilrements
All students including SMWU’s exchange students are required to complete their payments upon arrival.
Visiting Students
Students who are not from exchange universities or from SMWU’s partner institution who were not selected as exchange students.
Before applying directly, it is recommended that students contact the international office of their home university to verify the transferability of credits earned at SMWU.
Exchange Students
SMWU’s partner institution students must be nominated by their home university as exchange candidates. All application documents should be submitted to SMWU through the international office of their home university. Individual applications are not accepted.
The following documents are required to Apply:

Benefits for International Students
Sookmyung Buddy Leadership Group, URINK
U.R.I. (United Relationship for Internationalization) is a student-led group at Sookmyung Women’s University. Local SMWU students volunteer as buddies to assist and support international students on campus. Each international student is paired with a student buddy who helps them with general matters in Korea and helps them adjust to university life. The program promotes cultural exchange, fosters lasting friendships, and offers opportunities for students to participate in various events and activities together.
Scholarship Offered Volunteer Programs
International students from around the world can volunteer in Sookmyung Women’s University’s English Speaking Spot (ESS) and Second Language Tutoring program (SLT). In this program, they have the opportunity to teach their native language to Sookmyung students and receive a scholarship of KRW 10,000 per hour throughout the semester. It is a great way for international students to share their language skills and earn a scholarship at the same time.

Student Exchange Program
CUK offers a coeducational international program and welcomes students to study for one or two semesters as an exchange student at CUK. This program is open to undergraduate students enrolled as full-time students at our partner institutions. During the program, students will have opportunities to experience Korean culture, and develop "global competence" through the multicultural environment that CUK offers.
Exchange students are those nominated by partner institutions which have formal exchange agreements with CUK. Therefore, before applying for the CUK Student Exchange Program, students are asked to contact the related office of their home institutions in advance. Students are required to follow the process mentioned below.
Application Procedures for Spring 2025
Application Procedures for Spring 2022
Nomination
Period
26 August ~ 25 October 2024
Procedure
It must be completed by a staff who in charge of student exchange program
Application
Period
30 October ~ 17 November 2024
Procedure
Students need to complete the online application and also post documents to CUK OIA
*Link for online application will be accessable from 17 November 2024
*Hard copies of all application document must arrive to CUK no later than 27 December 2024
Admission
Period
First week of January 2025
Procedure
Certificate of Admission(CoA) will be issued and sent to student by email
*Hard copies(original documents) must be submitted before issuing the CoA
Important Dates for Spring 2025
Important Dates for Spring 2022

Course Change Period: 1st week of the semester
Dormitory Move-in
A week before the semester begins
Orientation
A week before the semester begins

Spring Semester Ends

Official Transcript Issuance
Early July 2025
Academic year
Spring semester
begins in the early March
Fall semester
begins in the late August
Duration of classes
16 weeks per semester
Duration of exchange
One semester or two semesters (one full year)
Language of instruction
Exchange students can study either 100% in English, 100% in Korean or mixing classes in both languages if their level is good enough
Grading
Students will receive a letter grade ranging from A+ to F. The grade of “A” is given for excellent performance; “B” for above average; “C” for average; “D” for minimally passing performance; and “F” for failure. In addition, “+” and “0“ are used for further differentiation. A student’s performance with “+” indicates a superior performance in that letter grade, and “0“ indicates a slightly weaker performance in that letter grade. Other grades include “P” (pass) and “F” (fail). The grade will become a part of permanent record at CUK.
Transcripts
Credits earned at CUK can be transferred. Please consult with your study abroad advisor or academic advisor at your home institution for regulations concerning credit transfer. The official transcript will be sent to the home institution of an exchange student automatically. If you request more copies, you should pay for the transcript issuance fee and delivery fee.

A형(영) | M5: This course is designed to provide a broad introduction to global environmental challenges we face today. It will cover several global environmental topics such as climate change, biodiversity, marine pollution, hazardous waste and trans-boundary air pollution. It will also cover issues in environmental law and international trade law. 
A6: Central Liberal Studies Required | B6: Catholic College | C6: 06819 | D6: Global Health from Multidisciplinary Perspectives | E6: Global Health from Multidisciplinary Perspectives | F6: 01 | G6: Freshman | H6: 3/3 | I6: 32 | J6: 김민우 | K6: MON1~3(N405) | L6: English(A type)
A형(영) | M6: The course will introduce students to the main concepts of the global health field and enhance their understandings in the social, economic, cultural, legal, and political processes by which global health policy influences global health objectives. Students will be able to discuss the social, political and economic determinants of global health and identify the evolving national institutions, international organizations, private interests, and global partnerships structuring global health policy. Students will further analyze the ethical, moral and legal norms that frame global health governance and evaluate global health policy to address disease prevention and health promotion. Potential topics to be explored include basic research methods in global health, health systems and management, infectious diseases and epidemics, global nutrition and agriculture, child health, sexual and reproductive health, humanitarian aid, environmental health, conflict, culture, and gender, etc.

A10: First Major Electives | B10: Spatial Design  & Consumer Studies | C10: 07101 | D10: 공간디자인기초실습 | E10: Spatial Design Foundation | F10: 01 | G10: Freshman | H10: 4/3 | I10: 2 | J10: 김나연 | K10: TUE2~5(D208) | L10: English(B type)
B형(영) | M10: This course serves as an introductory major course in Spatial Design, offering fundamental practical experience in English.

The primary objective of this course is to comprehensively understand various spatial environments where life occurs and to enhance the necessary perspectives, theoretical knowledge, and spatial design expression skills needed to create them. We aim to broaden our perspective on how we perceive spatial environments in our daily lives, foster creative thinking, interdisciplinary abilities, and expressive skills to create improved spaces.

Throughout this course, students will practice exercises that involve expressing spaces using architectural elements, with the goal of developing perceptual and creative potential in relation to spaces. Students will gain experience in the basic architectural language of form required to create spaces accommodating human behavior, analyze spatial meanings, and cultivate spatial expression abilities during the design process. Additionally, the course aims to enhance conceptual idea development, visual communication skills, and provide fundamental practice in spatial design, ultimately contributing to a broader understanding of architecture and interior design as a whole.

● to observe and gain an understanding of the physical characteristics of the spatial environments in which we reside
● to understand architects’ philosophy, design concepts, and spatial drawings through the examination of global architectural works
● to understand spatial scale and design elements while acquiring the skills necessary for architectural representation techniques and 3D model making (including sketching, drawing, diagrams, photography, collage, 3D study models, etc.).
● to foster the design development of spatial concept ideas and enhance visual communication skills
● to Acquire knowledge of spatial design methods, fundamental components, and the overall design process.

B형(영) | M11: 
This course focuses on acquiring the fundamental and essential mathematical tools required for specialized studies in Biologics Engineering. Moving beyond general mathematical concepts, it specifically educates students on the core principles of differential equations, linear algebra, and basic statistics necessary for solving practical engineering problems such as bioreactor modeling, pharmacokinetic analysis, and biological system data processing. Students will strengthen their quantitative reasoning skills through this course, enabling them to analytically model and predict complex bioengineering phenomena using real-world examples from the biologics field.

A12: First Major Electives | B12: 바이오로직스공학부 | C12: 07584 | D12: 의료용고분자공학개론 | E12: Introduction to Biomedical Polymer Engineering | F12: 01 | G12: Freshman | H12: 3/3 | I12: 0 | J12: 양대혁 | K12: MON6(N103), WED4~5(N103) | L12: English(B type)
B형(영) | M12: This course is designed for students who have selected or are considering Biologics Engineering as their major. It aims to enhance their understanding of biomedical polymers, which serve as the fundamental basis for the delivery of biopharmaceutical raw materials. By taking this course, students will be provided with opportunities for proper academic exploration and informed major selection. Furthermore, it will establish a solid foundation in drug delivery systems (DDS), ensuring sufficient comprehension for future advanced coursework related to biopharmaceuticals.

Q
[Academic Records] Grading
A.
Students will receive a letter grade
ranging from A+ to F. The grade of “A” is given for excellent performance; “B”
for above average; “C” for average; “D” for minimally passing performance; and
“F” for failure. In addition, “+” and “0“ are used for further differentiation.
A student’s performance with “+” indicates a superior performance in that
letter grade, and “0“ indicates a slightly weaker performance in that letter
grade. Other grades include “P” (pass) and “F” (fail). The grade will become a
part of permanent record at CUK.
9
Q
[Courses Registration] Is there any other information that I should know?
A.
Students
cannot drop any official grades including classes that received an ‘F.’
Therefore, make sure to attend all classes on the first week of school and if
there are any courses you would like to drop, you may add or drop courses
during the “C
lass Schedule Change Period”.
8
Q
[Courses Registration] Can I withdrawal the courses after the “Class Schedule Change Period”?
A.
Students
may withdrawal from enrolled courses during the given period, by the 4
th
of week of September without penalty. However, please keep in mind that course
addition is not allowed during this period.
The
students are required to have their withdrawn courses approved by the course
professor for the process to be completed. In addition, the “Class Schedule
Change Form” must be submitted to the department you belong to, during this
period. If not, students may face academic penalty such as receiving an “F”
grade for the course.
7
Q
[Courses Registration] Can I change the courses after registration on orientation?
A.
Students
may add or drop courses during the “C
lass Schedule Change Period”
(the first week of the semester), by
logging in to the school website called Trinity System.
6
Q
[Courses Registration] Is there a maximum of credits I can register for?
A.
Students
can take almost all courses offered at undergraduate level from 9 credits up to
a maximum of 19 credits per semester. If you register less than 9 credits you
must submit an statement of reasons to Office of International Affairs.
5

A.
In
the third week of August (around Aug 10~14), there will be a course
registration date, in that period, most students will self-quarantine.

Q
[Dormitory] Toiletries
A.
Toiletries can be purchased at the
nearest convenience store or market here.
19
Q
[Dormitory] What do I need when moving into the dorm?
A.
Students will need to bring their own
pillow, linens, blankets, towels, and toiletries.
18
Q
[Dormitory] When can I move in and move out?
A.
It is available from 9AM to 10PM at
the end of the August (the exact date will be notice). Please be sure to keep
your time, as it may not be possible to move into in other times.
Students who chose a 16-weeks plan,
have to move out by 14th December 2019. Students, chose a 24-weeks plan, have
to move out by the mid of February. If students chose a 16-week plan at first and
changed to a 24-week plan after arriving in Korea, students should leave the
dormitory for 7 to 10 days, dormitory cleaning period, right after the fall
semester. Please choose carefully.
17
Q
[Korean Language Class] How much is the tuition fee?
A.
Students from our partner universities
could receive a 30% discount. So, the tuition is KRW 910,000.
However, Korean language courses are
offered free of charge to every partner university which offers free language
courses to CUK students, following the reciprocity principle. In this case, Tuition
exemption applies only to Spring and Fall semesters. For summer and winter
semester, KRW 910,000 is required.
16
Q
[Korean Language Class] How does Korean language class work?
A.
Our Korean Language Education Center(KLEC)
offers Korean language classes at several different levels from beginner(level
1) to advance(level 6). Students will be assigned in accordance with their
placement test results. The placement test includes writing and an interview.
Beginners with no Korean background are also required to take the test. Korean
classes are offered 4 hours a day, from 9:00 am to 1:00 pm, Monday through
Friday. A total of 10 weeks and 200 hours of classes are offered.
15
Q
[Attendance] Regarding Absence Waivers for a menstrual period
A.
Female
students may use an absence waiver once a month
, by logging in to the school website called Trinity
System.
14
Q
[Attendance] Regarding Attendance for the Korean Language Education Center
A.
Korean language classes are 200 hours
in total for 10 weeks. If you miss more than 20 hours, you will not be able to
pass.
13
Q
[Attendance] Attendance for Regular Courses
A.
It is
an automatic F, when students are absent more than 1/4 of the classes. If students
suddenly become sick and cannot attend classes, it is needed to tell the course
professor. In addition, students should bring medical records and other
documents to discuss with the course professor whether there is any way that it
will not be treated as absent.
12
Q
[Academic Records] How many credits can I transfer?
A.
Credits earned at CUK can be
transferred. Please consult with your study abroad advisor or academic advisor
at your home institution for regulations concerning credit transfer.
11
Q
[Academic Records] How can I get my transcript?
A.
Transcripts will be sent to the
International Affairs of your school after the end of the semester. Students
who are enrolled for one year will have transcripts sent at the end of the
second semester. If you request more copies, you should pay for the transcript
issuance fee and delivery fee.

Q
[Dormitory] When can I make the payment for dormitory fee?
A.
The dormitory office will inform you the
specific payment schedule and method after you arrive. It is acceptable only by
domestic wire transfer. Please bring cash or withdraw KRW from ATM and visit
Woori Bank, located in the 1st floor of the International Hub Building, makes the
payment.
Please check the dormitory fee below;
General residents (16 weeks)
Long-term residents (24 weeks)
Double
KRW 1,248,000
KRW 1,835,000
3-Bed
KWR 1,040,000
KRW 1,529,000
4-Bed
KRW 790,000
KRW 1,161,000
Before
leaving your country, please be sure to check whether you can withdraw money
from Korea ATMs and withdrawal limit in a day.
31
Q
[Dormitory]  Cleaning Period
A.
The dorm cleaning period is for about 7-10
days right after the end of the fall semester and just before the start of the
spring semester. If you selected a 16-weeks plan at first and changed to a 24-weeks
plan after arrival at CUK, you must leave out the dorm for this period. The
dormitory office will offer temporary accommodation on campus during this
period at a reasonable price.
If you selected a 24-weeks plan from
the start, you don't have to leave at this time. However, you have to leave the
dormitory during the cleaning period just before the spring semester starts.
The dormitory will offer temporary accommodation at reasonable prices.

[Dormitory] Dormitory Rules & Regulations or any other dormitory information
A.
It is for a student who use a room for
4 students(4-bed room). If you use the top of a double deck bed, you are
supposed use the desk close to the window. If you use the bottom of a double
deck bed, you are supposed to use the desk near the door.
※
If there are two foreign students in a
quad room (a room for 4 students), the two foreign students should use only one
side only (bed 1,3 or bed 2,4)

From 1.am to 5.am.

smoke. Anybody caught breaking this rule will be out of the dormitory right
away.

text:
【第1頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
Institute of International Cooperation and Education (IICE). UOS Partner Information.

【第2頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
University of Seoul (UOS). University of Seoul, Institute of International Cooperation and Education. 163 Seoulsiripdae-ro, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea 02504.

【第3頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
Academic Year 2023. Spring Semester, 2023: Orientation February 28, 2023; Classes begin March 2, 2023; Classes end June 21, 2023; Nomination Deadline October 15, 2022; Application Deadline October 31, 2022. Fall Semester, 2023: Orientation August 31, 2023; Classes begin September 1, 2023; Classes end December 21, 2023; Nomination Deadline April 15, 2023; Application Deadline April 30, 2023. Tuition is paid to the home university, and in most cases, the application and documentation fee is waived.

【第4頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
Nominated students are required to complete UOS online application. What to submit on arrival: (1) One official photo (3.5cm x 4.5cm, full color with white background) for alien registration. (2) Certificate of Health, TB test result (or Chest X-ray) (it is a mandatory document only for on-campus housing residents and required to submit to housing office at check-in). Mostly Korean, but some of classes lectured in English. We cannot guarantee the courses your students would like to take. Language requirements (i.e.TOEFL scores): N/A. Applicants should have good commend of either Korean or English.

【第5頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
Undergraduate students should have completed at least two terms of university studies. All the courses offered at graduate level are taught in Korean. For the graduate students who are not fluent in Korean is strongly advised to be enrolled to undergraduate program. In this case, the student should ask his/her study abroad coordinator at the home university if this option would be accepted according to the university's policy. Recommended credit points per semester: 15 credits. A student should take at least 6 credits and can take up to 20 credits.

【第6頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
D-2 visa holders are automatically included in the mandatory National Health Insurance program. All international students are required to pay the Health Insurance Fee for Int'l Students every month from alien registration date. ex) Monthly contributions for international students for 2022: 56,030KRW. The Certificate of Health is required to be submitted to on-campus housing office for those who stay on-campus housing.

【第7頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
UOS only secure/guarantee on-campus housing only for those exchange students whose universities secure/guarantee on-campus housing for UOS students. UOS do not secure on-campus housing to all partner universities for dormitory room shortage. Please confirm with your home university coordinator your housing option before complete UOS online application. Residence Hall: Each room of double occupancy. Fees: 636,000KRW/semester + 100,000KRW deposit = 736,000KRW. Fees for vacation (about 2 months): 435,000 KRW.

【第8頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
International House: Each unit with 2 rooms / 3 rooms / 5 rooms of single occupancy. Fees: 912,000KRW/semester + 100,000KRW deposit = 1,012,000KRW. Fees for vacation (about 2 months): 435,000KRW fee. Curfew between 3 a.m. and 5 a.m. Fees are payable on arrival at UOS. Above information is subject to change. Off-campus housing is a contractual matter between students and accommodation, and the UOS IICE is not involved at all.

【第9頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
Scholarship can be offered on condition that your home university provides similar benefits for UOS students in return. If yes, how much is it? (200,000 KRW to 400,000 KRW per month). The recipients should stay in Korea more than 15 days per month to receive this scholarship. UOS scholarship is not provided during vacations (July&August / January&February).

【第10頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
Estimated costs: 800,000 KRW - 1,000,000 KRW per month. Including food, local transportation, books, entertainment, etc. Exchange students will hear from SeoulMate by email about a month before each semester starts. UOS's location in Seoul: 10km away from City Hall (North East Seoul). Above information is subject to change.

【第11頁】

【同SHA、同頁人工視覺核對摘錄，非全文轉錄；116適用性未核實】
UOS Partner Information. Institute of International Cooperation and Education IICE.

3. FIRE PREVENTION
- Do not smoke in the building including toilet, lounge, balcony, etc.
- Devices not in use must be plugged off.
-   Possession or usage of electrical heating appliances, any flammable 
and hazardous materials are strictly prohibited in dormitory.
- Learn the general principles of using the fire extinguisher.

text:

Courses offered in English
Exchange students can take up to 20 credits for a regular semester (spring or     fall) and up to 8credits for Seoul International Summer School. Most of the     courses offered during regular semesters are lectured in Korean, which can be     found at
UOS Website → Academics → Colleges → Courses
Courses List
List of Courses offered in English
→ Please click each course title and you can find its course description
→ The course list below is provided for reference only, and         the courses offered may vary each semester. Course availability depends on         individual course registration results, and enrollment is not guaranteed.         Therefore, we recommend that you keep flexibility in your academic planning.
→ Please note that major-specific courses offered by certain         departments—such as Architecture, Design, and Music—require prior         approval. If you wish to enroll in major courses from these departments, you         must confirm the availability after the course list is finalized each semester.

2026 Fall

The Courses Lectured in English for Regular Semesters
Department
Course No
Course Title
Credit
Department of Sport Science
63011
Introduction to Adapted Physical Activity
This course is designed to provide an introduction to the field of adapted physical activity for exercise and sport science majors. The goal of this course is to gain a better understanding of various disability conditions and how physical activity can be accommodated to unique conditions of individuals with disabilities. This course covers legislation, etiology, principles and problems related to adapted physical activity programs, as well as sports for individuals with disabilities.
3
Department of Design
66350
Visual Communication DesignⅡ
This course is designed to develop well-organized visual abilities (especially 2D) and create a matured view of the production process of visual design to fit the concept.
3
School of Economics
28168
Economics of corporate finance
This course is for undergraduate students who have basic knowledge of economic concepts and methodologies, and covers the topics of capital structure and financial decision making under the valuation framework to provide understanding of corporate finance theory.
3
School of Economics
28015
Econometrics
Econometrics is a collection of research methods used to estimate and test economic relationships. The methods introduced in this course are also widely applied in business disciplines, including accounting, finance, marketing, and management, as well as in many areas of the social sciences.                               This course is designed to help bridge the gap between being “a student of economics” and becoming “a practicing economist.” Through this course, you will develop a broad understanding of the field and build intuition for how econometric methods work. The course will emphasize both a clear understanding of fundamental econometric tools and their practical application to real-world data and economic questions.                                                    By the end of this course, students should be comfortable with fundamental concepts in statistics and probability. They should be able to estimate and interpret linear regression models, critically evaluate regression results reported in applied academic research, and clearly explain empirical findings to audiences without formal training in economics.
3
School of Economics
28148
Asset pricing theory
The purpose of this course is to provide an opportunity to study the fundamental theory of pricing financial assets as an application of economic models and analytical frameworks.                               The use of AI is permitted in class, but its use in exam is strictly prohibited.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40138
Electrical and Computer Engineering Capstone Design
The main objective is to learn design and implementation methods for software projects. The students will follow an object-oriented software design process. During the first half of a semester, each team of two students will work on a different project. During the second half, each team is assigned to a part of a large project. To emphasize cooperative design and communication skills, students are required to have regular project meetings, make presentations, and publish associated documents. The students should be familiar with object-oriented programming.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
30034
Introduction to Algorithm
This course introduces the design and analysis of basic computer algorithms. Students will understand worst-case running time for an algorithm and its associated data structure. Covered topics are: sorting, searching, dynamic programming and advanced data structure.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40063
Signals and Systems
The objective of this course is to introduce the analytical tools and techniques needed for the design and analysis of continuous-time linear systems. The primary topics are convolution, transforms and sampling theory. Specifically, this course covers topics associated with the continuous time systems; classification of signals and systems, convolution, differential equations, Fourier series, Fourier transform, bilateral Laplace transform, and design and analysis of continuous-time linear systems with linear circuit examples. We also will discuss the introductory topics related with the discrete-time systems; Nyquist sampling theory, discrete-time processing of the continuous-time signals.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40070
Digital Signal Processing
The objective of this course is to present the analytical tools needed for the design and analysis of discrete-time systems. We will cover classifications of discrete-time signals and systems, convolution, difference equations. Also, this course deals with several transforms including bilateral Z-transforms, discrete-time Fourier transform, Discrete Fourier transform. Several tools for analyzing discrete-time signals and systems will be introduced in this course so that students can acquire the ability of analyzing and designing discrete-time systems.  Several topics will be given as programming projects to provide the experiences on the practical system design.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40087
Artificial Intelligence
This course introduces artificial intelligence problems and techniques applicable to intelligent systems. Topics included are: intelligent agents, problem solving, knowledge and reasoning, planning, uncertain knowledge and reasoning, and learning.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40095
Solid-State Physical Electronics
The lecture will provide a valuable theoretical introduction and an overview of the fundamental physics of solids, in particular semiconductors. This course includes crystal properties, atoms and electrons, Energy bands of semiconductors, and p-n junction structures.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40106
Embedded Systems Applications Design
This class covers the co-design of hardware and software which is the essential technology for the design of embedded systems. The kernel design, the device driver design, the I/O system design, and the VHDL design are introduced in this class.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40127
Applied Microprocessor Lab
In this experimental lecture, the fundamental operation, designing the peripheral circuit, and programming of microprocessor will be covered. Students will practice designing microprocessor peripheral circuits with FPGA. For term-project they have to design, and make microprocessor system and install OS into the microprocessor circuit.
2
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40137
Fabrication of Integrated Circuit
Integrated Circuits have been extensively employed in a variety of wide applications such as memory, communications systems, medical devices, home and industrial appliances. Recent rapid growth in electronics fields shows that Integrated Circuits play a more and more important role in next-generation automobiles, sensors, merged memory logic, and non-memory system applications.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40140
Introduction to Power Electronics
Students will learn fundamentals of the power diodes and switches for power conversion at the beginning. The topics of this class extend to analysis and design methods of the DC to DC, AC to DC, and DC to AC power converters using the power diodes and switches.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
40166
Artificial Intelligence for Cellular Communications
This class offers various topics including overview of cellular communications and wireless channel characteristics, and highlights network architectures and fundamental technologies for cellular communication systems. Especially, this class emphasizes artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and services for 6G cellular communication systems. In addition, this class includes the following topics for prediction and classification in cellular communication environments: linear regression model, linear classification model, neural networks, and so on.
3
Department of Materials Science and Engineering
39044
Thermodynamics of Materials
The 1st, 2nd, and 3rd laws of thermodynamics are introduced, and then the reaction equilibria between condensed phase and gas phase and theory of solutions are studied.
3
Department of Materials Science and Engineering
39115
Materials Capstone Design
This course provides training on critical thinking and engineering design. The students are challenged to innovate and improve materials used in any engineering systems, and are also encouraged to pursue interdisciplinary studies. The students’ designs are expected to be creative enough to be filed as an international patent application so that their intellectual properties can be protected. Also, selected designs will be competed at international expositions.
3
Department of Materials Science and Engineering
39140
Design of Experiments for Materials AI
This course integrates computer programming skills with statistical data analysis and experimental design, which are essential foundations for scientific research and decision making, to understand basics of artificial intelligence.  Students will apply these techniques to an engineering design project at the end of the semester.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51250
Concepts and Uses of English Grammar
This course aims to give students a good understanding of how grammar is conceptualized and used in authentic contexts. Students learn the grammar of spoken and written English, improving their knowledge of English grammar. There are 15 sections; each section covers one area of English grammar like tenses, modals, nouns, verbs, determiners, finite clauses, non-finite clauses, conditionals, reported speech, and the like. Each section focuses on its uses of a grammatical pattern, and practical exercises and also explores grammatical contrasts between apparent similar grammatical patterns.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51252
AI and Logic in English
This course aims to introduce the intersection of artificial intelligence, theoretical semantics, and natural language logic. Students will learn various topics, including fundamental concepts of semantics and logic, principles of natural language processing, word vectorization, context understanding, semantic analysis, and logical form.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51257
English and cultures of the world
This course aims to explore the interaction between English and English-speaking cultures around the world. Students will engage with authentic materials such as films, novels, newspapers, and broadcasts, covering not only well-known varieties of English such as American, British, and Australian English, but also English in lesser-known areas such as India, Singapore, European nations, etc. Through synchronic and diachronic analysis, the course examines how English has influenced different cultures and, in turn, how cultural, social, and historical contexts have shaped the use and development of English. By comparing diverse national cases, students will gain a critical understanding of the global status of English, its regional variations, and the significance of English in processes of globalization and in contemporary.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51068
English Phonetics
This course aims to provide students with a thorough grounding in general English phonetics and help them to develop a practical ability to use the knowledge. This course also supplements insight and understanding about the important principles of American English pronunciation, through which they will acquire a theoretical and substantial basis for how English sounds are produced and how they are related with prosody such as stress and intonation. Students will have an opportunity to correct their pronunciation and finally have it evaluated.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51086
British and American Drama
This course is a survey of 19th and 20th century plays written by British and American playwrights. Representative dramatists from each literary-historical period and a range of dramatic style will be covered with the emphasis on modern drama. Along with analysis of dramatic texts, some attention will be paid to the theatrical, cultural and historical contexts. Selections from filmed productions will be shown periodically. The course will help students critically approach the cultural factors of performance texts and provide chances to interpret/rewrite/perform the plays from their own perspectives.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51193
Understanding of English Education
The present course is for students who are interested in learning how to teach English as Second Language effectively. It covers the theory and practice of teaching listening, speaking, reading, writing, vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, discourse and assessment.                               Based on the knowledge they have acquired, students will analyze the current English textbooks used in secondary schools in Korea. They will identify the problems in the textbooks and possibly come up with the solution and detailed suggestions.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51201
English Presentation and Discussion
The course aims to study and learn the skills necessary to make a clear, well-organized, and successful presentation and discussion by strengthening their oral and aural English skills. They gain experience and confidence in being an active discussion participant and leader as well as a strong presenter.
3
Department of English Language and Literature
51223
English Practice
The primary objective of this course is to help students develop their speaking abilities and communicative competence through use of the language. To meet this aim, ample opportunities to practice the language by speaking in class and interacting with others will be provided. Although the major skills we will focus on are discussion and presentation, competence in other types of communication such as debates and surveys are also a part of the curriculum. Although the course is open to students of any level, the course is quite demanding in terms of the work required. Only students are willing and eager to put in a lot of work to develop their skills are encouraged to enroll. NOTE: This course SHOULD NOT be taken along with "English Interview & Presentation" (영어면접과발표) during the same semester.
3
Department of Statistics
47771
Machine Learning and Lab
In this course, learning methods based on R or Python often adopted in various learning problems are introduced. The topics includes supervised learning methods such as decision trees and neural networks and unsupervised learning methods such as association rules, clustering, and dimension reduction methods.
3
Department of Physics
45040
Physics and Computer II
In this course students will learn scientific programming. Short lectures on C++ will be given. Students will learn various aspects of OO languages, such as class design, inheritance, templates, File I/O, and data modeling, Students must successfully finish the series class, Physics and Computer I, in order to follow this course correctly.
3
Department of Physics
45111
Solid State PhysicsⅡ
This course is designed to study advanced topic of solid state materials including superconducting devcice (SQUID), para- and ferroelectricity, ferro- and antiferromagnetism, magnetic resonance, non-crystalline solid and point defect physics, surface and interface physics , also basic aspects of nano-size materials.
3
Department of Physics
45153
Applied Physics Experiment
The development and applications of Galileo's telescope gave birth to the field of optics. These laser and optical technologies have been used as the most important tools in physics, making it possible to experimentally prove numerous scientific phenomena and applied in many engineering fields.
3
College of Business Administration
27002
Accounting Principles
The course covers the objectives, basic theories, principles, and methods of accounting.  Students will measure and report financial positions regarding income, costs, and revenue. The course includes the framework for decision-making, recording processes, and accounting cycles.
3
College of Business Administration
27102
Consumer Behavior
This course aims to explore the importance of consumer behavior analysis from various perspectives in consumer-centered modern marketing, introducing models of consumer behavior from a behavioral science standpoint and researching the application and evaluation of each model. To achieve this, students will acquire and understand the theories and analytical techniques related to social and psychological factors in consumer information evaluation and decision-making processes, and develop the ability to apply these to real-world decision-making situations faced by consumers.
3
College of Business Administration
27105
Marketing Management
This course takes an analytical approach to the study of marketing problems of business firms and other organizations. Focus is placed on the influence of the marketplace and the marketing environment on marketing decision making; the determination of an organization's products, prices, channels and communication strategies; and an organization's system for planning and controlling its marketing efforts.
3
College of Business Administration
27301
Financial Management
The major topics of this course are as follows: the decision of the size of capital required by the firm, the planning about the timing and method of borrowing such capital, the optimal operation and management of the capital, and the theories and practices about these topics.
3
College of Business Administration
27302
Investment Theory
In this class, you will understand why you should invest in stocks. As an overarching concept, we learn that there are two types of risk in financial markets: good risks with expected returns and bad risks without expected returns. Portfolio theory teaches that investors can eliminate bad risk through diversification. The Nobel Prize-winning CAPM theory shows the relationship between good risk and expected return. Finally, we understand that it is very difficult to predict the direction of future stock prices through the efficient market hypothesis, which states that stock prices fully and immediately reflect relevant information.
3
College of Business Administration
27407
Human Resource Management
In a knowledge-driven global economy, organizations and managers have increasingly recognized that a critical source of competitive advantage stems from having an effective human resource system for obtaining, mobilizing, and managing the organization’s human resources. It is imperative that organizations understand the key HRM functions and how these functions should be aligned in order to gain competitive advantage through their people. Human Resource Management issues begin to appear from the very moment you hire someone for the first time, or you are hired by someone forthe first time. You will likely spend a major part of your life working for organizations as an employee, or, perhaps, leading one you have started. Also, you could become an HR professional. In any case, however, your knowledge and understanding on human resource management will help you succeed in your career, as an employee, a top manager, a business owner, or an HR professional.
3
College of Business Administration
27503
Managerial Accounting
This course covers the preparation and analysis of cost concepts, theories, and the implementation and evaluation of an accounting system as a source of information for internal users.   This course also includes an overview of decision making, planning, controlling, and evaluation of an organization.
3
College of Business Administration
27701
Management Information Systems
You will be ready and able to understand key business models, concepts, frameworks, and issues concerning IS and their use in business. You will be able to assess the current uses and value of IS in an organization, identify where IS can provide strategic advantage, and identify where firms and markets are vulnerable to being disrupted or severely compromised. You will have an understanding of the role of data, information, and knowledge in supporting the decision-making activities of the organization. You will be able to demonstrate how Excel and Access can be used for modeling and solving business problems.
3
College of Business Administration
27940
Financial Markets
The purpose of this course is to develop an understanding of the modern theory of financial intermediation so that the students can have conceptual and practical knowledge and skills for analyzing financial institutions and markets. There are three basic concepts to learn in this course: 1) information asymmetry, 2) risk in financial intermediation and 3) management of financial risk and related regulation. A considerable time will be spent on combining theories of information asymmetry and financial intermediation and their practical applications.
3
College of Business Administration
27964
Corporate Finance
This course is designed to help you develop a deeper understanding of the issues and the basic tools needed for corporate finance managers. The issues addressed in this course include how corporations raise capital, capital structure decisions, corporate valuations, mergers and acquisitions, and corporate governance. It is designed for students who has taken financial management course. This course will cover many cases on the issues being covered in the class.
3
Department of Urban Administration
11130
Urban Regeneration
"This course examines urban redevelopment and regeneration with particular attention being paid to the integration of quality of life-related considerations (e.g. urban aesthetics, walkability, culture) into revitalization efforts at the city, district and neighbourhood scale. The course will begin with a chronological survey of some of the most notable examples of urban redevelopment in the western world, including Haussmann’s renovation of Paris in the 19th century and Burnham’s visionary plan for Chicago in the early 20th century. We will then address how culture has been revisited in recent decades in urban design, planning, and development alongside notions of creativity and sustainability. In particular, urban redevelopment and regeneration will be addressed through the lens of specific policy and planning themes each week, such as modernist cities, creative cities, and healthy cities."
3
Department of Architecture
41622
Theory of Housing and Settlement
Housing is a container of family life and a formal constituent of dwelling culture. It reflects cultivation of nature, organization of family and communities, and foundation of institutions and orders. Students gain an understanding of spatial diversity and temporal transition in urban housing. Based on the relationship between behavior forms and housing types on which collective ideas are imprinted, students learn the typological issues of architectural design. It provides broad knowledge on the ways housing planning and design contribute to residents’ adjustment to the environment. An in-depth study on the formal development of Korean agricultural housing shall be conducted.
3
Department of Architecture
46088
Architectural Design 4 (Capstone Design)
This course explores collective building forms in relation to the urban context. Focusing on public discourse, district-unit planning, and landscape regulations, it examines density, volume, and external spaces shaped by building complexes. From individual units to the urban edge, integrated master planning and architectural design are addressed.
6
Department of Chinese Language and Culture
65101
Chinese Conversation in Intermediate Level
This course, a continuation of "Chinese Conversation in Elementary Level," aims to help students acquire intermediate-level Chinese skills.
3
Department of Chinese Language and Culture
65103
Current Issues in Contemporary China
In this course, students will develop their ability to understand and discuss current issues in China in Chinese, utilizing the knowledge of Chinese language, society, and history that they have acquired in previous years of study.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90001
Special Topics in Korean Studies
This course aims to provide a better understanding of Korean society and its culture. Through the course activities and also by performing an individual research on the topic oftheir own interests, students are expected to enhance their comprehension of Korean society and culture. The students will understand the value system and the world view of Korean society and use the key concepts to analyze the contemporary issues including feminism, minority rights, environmental issues, inter-cultural conflicts and politics-business ties and so on.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90002
Korean History
This course is designed to provide an introductory knowledge of Korean history. Students will acquire a general knowledge of Korean history as a whole and gain an understanding of important historical features. The course will focus on modern history and its influence on present day Korea. The students will acquire the basic understanding of Korean history from the ancient time to the modern time with the focus on the pre-modern and the modern history so that the students can confidently answer to some of the important questions regarding Korean history such as (1) how were the relationships with its neighboring countries before the modernization, (2) how Korea was colonized by the Imperial Japan,(3) why was Korea divided into the north and the south (4) why did the Korean War break out(5) How did Korea achieve its economic and political developments and so on.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90003
Korean Tradition and Culture
This course aims to provide a better understanding of Korean tradition and culture. Through the course activities and also by performing an individual research on the topic of their own interests, students are expected to enhance their comprehension of Korean society and culture. The students will acquire the basic understanding in the Korean religions and values in order to comprehend the Korean traditions and culture in various areas including music, dance, painting, printing, food, architecture, national treasures, seasonal customs and so on.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90004
Korean Politics and Society
Introducing major topics and issues of Korean Politics after 1945, the course deals with the varying tendency of Korean Democracy and following social changes.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90005
Korean Economy & Business.
"The Korean economy has experienced rapid economic growth of roughly 10% annual growth from 1963 to 1991. This lecture examines factors that have enabled this rapid growth with respect to labor, capital, and technological progress, Korean conglomerate (Chaebol)."
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90006
Mass Media and Popular Culture in Korea
The course deals with an influence of Mass media to Popular culture in Korean.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90009
East Asian History
This course is designed to develop the student's understanding of East Asian history from the prehistoric ages to the modernization era In this course, students will learn about an everfast growing and changing East Asian society focusing on the inter-relations among China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam. The students will have an overview of East Asian history from the prehistoric ages to the modernization era with the focus on the beginning of the Chinese civilization,the inter-state relationship between China and its neighboring states, the tri-angula relationship among China, Japan and Korea during the pre-modern and the modernization period.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90010
Economic Development in East Asia
The development experience in East Asia varies greatly. The eight high-performing East Asian economies include three models of development;the manufactured export-led, state interventionist model of Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan; the free port, commercial center model of Singapore and HongKong; and the natural resource-rich model of Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand. Also the transitional models of China and Vietnam are included in the performers. It is thus difficult to generalize the true cause ofthe East Asian economic development.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90203
Urban Economics and policy
This class is designed for students to be equipped with a framework to diagnose and address urban problems in economic perspectives. It also aims to enhance the students’ understanding of economical logics behind policies on land, housing, real estate, urban finance and transportation. At the end ofthis course, students are expected to - understand economic basis of public intervention in urban policies - understand urban structure of various metropolitan cities in different contexts
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90205
Politics and Diplomacy of the two Koreas
This course is an introduction to the political development and foreign relations of South Korea (the Republic of Korea, ROK) and North Korea (the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, DPRK). The course explores the evolution of political and diplomatic issues in and between twoKoreas as well as the legacies of national division.Topics include Korean War, South Korea’s democratic development, inter-Korean relations and unification, North Korean nuclear crisis, South Korea’s inter-governmental and public diplomacy, among others. By the end ofthe course, students are expected to understand the key topics and issues dominating Korean politics and foreign relations.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90206
Special Topics in Global Business
The objective of this course is to provide the foundation of knowledge, skills, and tools necessary for effective global business consulting. Given this objective, this course will overview the consulting profession with a subsequent emphasis on organization consulting issues, including relevant theories, business models, communications or reporting skills, presentation skills and negotiation skills within the global business context. Throughout this course, an effort will be placed on developing and learning a wide range of interpretational global business field.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90207
Global Marketing Management
The purpose of this course is to help students advance on their own marketing careerjourney by enabling students to prepare themselves to become leaders of global marketing environment. Through lecture, readings and an examination of the case studies, the course is intended to illuminate the paths that others have taken and provide a spark for students ’ own marketing career development.We will also explore new ways of global marketing in today’s younger generation through TEAM projects. Marketing career development tools used in the course will be easily applicable for students and useful in the future.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90210
Pronunciation of Korean and its Application
This course is designed to help international students having various L1 backgrounds to correct their Korean pronunciation and improve speech communication in Korean. Students will learn the articulatory mechanisms of Korean vowels and consonants and the phonological principles and rules about various sound alternations. Moreover, students study intonation principles of Korean and practice applying them to their own speech, which will dramatically reduce foreign accent. in their Korean speaking. They will correct their Korean pronunciation and intonation through a vast amount of practice in class, taking advantage of the immersion environment out of class.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90211
Introduction to International Law
The purpose of this course is to provide a comprehensive framework for the analysis of contemporary public international law by drawing upon various theories and cases. Given that global society is developing rapidly, proper understanding of international community from legal perspective is essential for grasping the nature of global society. The goal of this course is to provide students with normative foundations and principles for assessing international legal issues.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90214
Lifetime Physical Activity I
Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: 1. demonstrate commitment to the activity through regular participations 2. demonstrate basic fundamental skills necessary for ultimate, badminton and pickleball games 3. demonstrate understanding of rules, terminology, and basic strategies necessary for ultimate, badminton and pickleball plays 4. demonstrate proper etiquette during game play of ultimate, badminton and pickleball 5. demonstrate interest in improving skills and conditioning in class 6. demonstrate knowledge of how to continue play ultimate, badminton and pickleball games outside of class
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90217
Special Issues in Business and Financial Accounting
This course is designed to learn both investment knowledge and business English by relevant situations for accountants/investment bankers/fund managers. Upon completion of this course, students will have gained strengths in speaking professional English by using BASIC terminologies in the real world. Students also will have practiced communication skills for speech presentations in the global accounting/investment banking/asset management field. Also a mock trading will be executed for understanding the equity markets
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90219
Special Issues in Entrepreneurship and Innovation
The objective of this course is to provide the foundation of knowledge, skills, and tools necessary for entrepreneurship and innovation. Given this objective, this course will overview the entrepreneurial mind-set with a subsequent emphasis on initiating entrepreneurial ventures and developing the entrepreneurial plan. Throughout this course, an effort will be placed on growing strategies for entrepreneurial ventures under a wide range of global/local business field.
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90221
Introduction to Korean Linguistics
"This course is an introductory course to Korean Linguistics for students without any background or previous knowledge of linguistics. Students will study different approaches to the analysis of the Korean language by covering following areas: Phonetics and Phonology, Morphology, Syntax, Semantics and Pragmatics. By the end of this course students will be able to gain deeper insights into and understanding of how Korean works and how we use it to communicate.                 *This course will be conducted in English.                 **You do not need to be fluent in Korean to take this course. However, you will find it hard to understand and tackle the course content without knowing the basics of the language."
3
Office of Int'l Affairs(OIA)
90222
Accounting with Cases
The course helps students develop a comprehensive understanding of how financial, cost, and managerial accounting concepts and principles are applied in both simulated and real-world business scenarios.
3
School of Electrical and Computer Engineering
92101
AI and Human Language
This course, offered under the AI Convergence Major, supports the expansion of AI education. It explores language, once seen as uniquely human, now challenged by AI, through engineering, humanities, cognitive science, and social sciences. By comparing human language and AI NLP, students practice creative integration of knowledge through texts, discussions, teamwork, and presentations in English.
3
School of Libertal Arts Education
01742
Chinese2
This course aims to enhance the basic Chinese language skills developed in the course. It focuses on explaining Chinese vocabulary, sentence patterns, and providing repetitive practice to improve communication skills in various situations. Students will develop a greater interest in the Chinese language and Chinese studies, and by gaining background knowledge about China during the course, they will be able to maintain their interest in both the language and Chinese culture. This course is linked to and allows students who have completed one semester of Chinese to study more advanced content. It will explain key expressions that can be used in various situations and provide opportunities for practical application through exercises.
3
School of Libertal Arts Education
01191
Cities and People
"This course will introduce students to some of the key issues that are typically covered in the broad field of urban studies. Emphasis will be placed on addressing global urbanization, the internal social and spatial structure of cities, and contemporary urban problems and potential solutions. Some of the specific topics to be discussed include the origins of cities, urban growth and decline, spatial models, suburban sprawl, place marketing and gentrification, poverty and crime, and current and projected challenges that face ‘sustainable city’ goals. By the end of this course, students will have an understanding of the historical evolution of cities as well as the contemporary changes that are occurring in cities around the globe. "
